title: ACL sync, drift and revocation
summary: Every copy of a permission (index, membership cache, answer cache) ages. Design how a change reaches each copy, how you detect copies that missed it, and what revocation time you promise per tier.
useIf: Permissions live in a source system and your index, caches or membership store hold copies of them.
avoidIf: You delegate retrieval to the source and keep no copy. Then there is nothing to sync, only a live call to rely on.

explain.md: A revoked grant keeps working until **every** copy catches up, and each copy ages at its own rate. A pull indexer cannot beat its next run: the schedule interval ranges from 5 to 1,440 minutes [[r19]]. Push ingestion lets you patch only the ACL field with `merge`, so revocation can be seconds, but then you own the change feed. Graph driveItem notifications average under a minute and can take up to six hours, and directory subscriptions expire in under 29 days and need renewal [[r27]]. Never promise a revocation time tighter than the slowest link.

Start by writing a **revocation target per sensitivity tier**. Restricted data may need seconds to minutes and general internal data may accept hours. These are planning estimates, not vendor numbers. Then list every copy of a permission (index ACL field, membership cache, answer cache, search replicas) and give each one an owner, a refresh mechanism and a way to detect when it is wrong.

explain.title: Chance a returned grant is stale

vars.v: revocations per grant per hour: the daily revocation rate divided by 24
hours between the source change and the index

explain.example: At 5% revocations a day and 24 hours of lag, P(stale) is about **4.9%** per returned grant, and with 10 hits about 39% of queries include a revoked document. At 1% a day and 1 hour of lag it is about 0.04% per grant, or about 0.4% of queries. Source: the lab model in the ACL decision space topic, a teaching simplification.

explain.title: Revocation includes deletes and caches
explain.md: Deleted source items must disappear from the index and from answer, semantic and membership caches. Test deletes, not only permission edits, with a canary document.

whereToUse: Setting a revocation target per sensitivity tier before building sync
SharePoint or lake content indexed on a schedule with permission fields
Security reviews that ask how fast a leaver loses access to answers
Incident response after a folder move or group rename left stale ACLs

use: Different tiers have different revocation targets
A copy of permissions exists in the index or a cache
You can sample and compare source and index ACLs
avoid: Quoting a single revocation number for the whole system
Relying on one mechanism for parent-scope and item-scope changes
Assuming a managed indexer means no drift
flips: Restricted data needs seconds: push merges from events plus a live check
Only general content is in scope: a scheduled indexer and a daily resync may be enough
Sources emit unreliable events: add delta-query reconciliation

pitfalls.symptom: A folder permission change never reaches the index
pitfalls.cause: Indexer runs pick up unique item ACLs but not parent-scope changes
pitfalls.fix: Trigger /resync with options permissions on change events and schedule one

pitfalls.cause: A Graph subscription expired after under 29 days
pitfalls.fix: Renew early, alert on missing events and reconcile with delta queries

pitfalls.symptom: Revoked users still see cached answers
pitfalls.cause: Answer or semantic caches are not scoped by ACL or outlive the target
pitfalls.fix: Key caches by ACL scope and set TTL below the revocation target

pitfalls.symptom: Deleted documents still appear in citations
pitfalls.cause: Deletes were not propagated to the index or caches
pitfalls.fix: Propagate tombstones by source id and test deletes with a canary

scenarios.title: General content, hours acceptable
scenarios.situation: An assistant covers 40 SharePoint sites of general internal content. Permissions rarely change, and leaving staff lose access to the source immediately. Hours of lag are acceptable to the business.
unknowns: How often do parent-scope permissions change?
scenarios.question: What sync design fits?

options.name: Indexer every few hours, a daily resync of permissions and a sampled drift audit
options.why: It matches an hours target at low cost and heals parent-scope changes through the resync [[r16]].
options.tradeoff: Stale grants for hours and a job to monitor.

options.name: Event-driven push pipeline with Graph subscriptions
options.tradeoff: Builds and runs a pipeline the target does not justify.

options.name: Indexer only, and assume the managed service keeps ACLs right
options.why: Parent-scope changes are not picked up by runs, so drift grows unseen.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for content where wrong access has no impact.

flips.if: A subset of sites turns restricted
flips.then: Give those sites event-driven updates and a live check.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the machinery to the revocation target.

scenarios.title: Restricted tier, seconds
scenarios.situation: A restricted tier in a custom push index must reflect a revoked grant within about ten seconds. The source emits change events through a webhook that occasionally drops messages.
unknowns: Is a live check allowed on restricted hits?
scenarios.question: How do you meet the target?

options.name: Nightly resync
options.why: A day of lag misses ten seconds by a wide margin.
options.tradeoff: Right for general content with a daily target.

options.name: Event-driven merge of the ACL field, a reconciliation job and a live check on restricted hits
options.why: Events give speed, reconciliation catches lost messages and the live check covers the gap [[r19]].
options.tradeoff: Three mechanisms to run and test.

options.name: Poll the source change feed every minute and merge
options.tradeoff: Up to a minute of lag, so ten seconds is missed.

flips.if: The target relaxes to five minutes
flips.then: A five-minute poll or indexer works.

flips.if: The source offers a reliable change feed with ordering

scenarios.takeaway: Seconds need events, healing and a live check.

scenarios.title: Drift found after a folder move
scenarios.situation: A daily sample finds that 0.3% of documents under a moved folder carry old ACLs in the index. Some of them are now more restricted at the source.
unknowns: How many documents are in the affected scope?
Can mismatched documents be hidden quickly?
scenarios.question: What do you do first?

options.name: Wait for the next scheduled run to fix it
options.why: Exposure continues, and parent-scope changes are not picked up by runs anyway.
options.tradeoff: Fine only for mismatches that grant less access.

options.name: Contain by hiding mismatched documents, run a targeted resync of the scope, then add a parent-scope event trigger
options.why: It stops exposure first, fixes the scope and removes the root cause.

options.name: Run a full re-index of the corpus immediately
options.tradeoff: Slow and expensive, and it does not contain exposure while it runs.

flips.if: Mismatches only grant less access than the source

flips.then: Open an incident and review logs.

scenarios.takeaway: Contain, repair the scope, then fix the cause.

scenarios.title: Deleted file still cited
scenarios.situation: A user deleted a sensitive file at the source. Two hours later the assistant still quotes it. The index sync runs every four hours and a semantic cache holds answers for a day.
unknowns: Do deletes propagate through the indexer?
scenarios.question: How do you close the gap?

options.name: Propagate deletes as tombstones by source id to the index and invalidate caches that cite it
options.why: It removes the chunks and every cached answer built from them.
options.tradeoff: Needs source ids on chunks and cache entries.

options.name: Shorten the cache TTL only
options.tradeoff: The index still serves the chunks until the next sync.

options.name: Wait for the next full rebuild
options.why: It leaves the document live for hours or days.

flips.if: The source supports soft deletes with events
flips.then: Use those events to trigger tombstones.

flips.if: Caches are keyed by ACL scope and short-lived

scenarios.takeaway: Revocation covers deletes, index copies and caches.

quiz.q: Using P(stale) = 1 - exp(-lambda x lag): 5% of grants are revoked per day (lambda = 0.05 / 24 per hour) and sync lag is 24 hours. What percentage of returned grants is stale?
quiz.explain: lambda times lag is 0.05, and 1 minus exp(-0.05) is about 0.049, or 4.9%. With 10 hits per query about 39% of queries contain a revoked document. It is a lab model, not a measurement.

quiz.q: A SharePoint library's permissions change at the folder level. The indexer runs every 5 minutes. What brings the index up to date?
options: A call to /resync with options permissions, or /resetdocs for specific keys
Waiting for the access token to expire
Nothing: SharePoint pushes folder changes to the index
quiz.explain: Runs pick up unique item ACL changes, but parent-scope changes need an explicit resync of permissions or a reset of specific documents.

quiz.q: Which statements set a realistic revocation expectation? Choose all that apply.
options: A pull indexer cannot update faster than its schedule interval of at least 5 minutes
Graph driveItem notifications can take up to six hours
Push ingestion can patch the ACL field immediately with merge
A managed indexer guarantees zero drift
quiz.explain: The schedule minimum is 5 minutes, driveItem notification latency has a six-hour maximum and push merge can update ACLs at once. No managed service guarantees zero drift.

flashcards.front: What is the revocation floor of a pull indexer?
flashcards.back: Its next run. The schedule interval is 5 to 1,440 minutes. Push ingestion can update ACLs immediately with merge but you own the change feed.

flashcards.front: How would you detect ACL drift?
flashcards.back: Sample documents daily, compare source and index ACLs, alert on any mismatch, hide mismatches until fixed, and chart the age of the oldest unsynced change.

flashcards.front: What does revocation include besides permission edits?
flashcards.back: Deletes and every cache: index chunks, answer caches, semantic caches and membership caches. Test with a canary document.
